question: Our full-time domestic help stole my mother's gold bangles from the locked cupboard while we were out and ran away. The police are saying it is a simple theft.
answer: The police are downplaying it. Theft by a servant or employee is an 'Aggravated Theft'. Under the BNS, this carries a significantly higher penalty (up to 7 years jail) compared to general theft, because it involves a breach of trust. Insist they file it under Section 305 BNS.

question: A local politician gave a speech in our colony yesterday explicitly telling people to boycott and attack shops owned by our community. People are already throwing stones today.
answer: This is legally classified as 'Hate Speech' that promotes enmity between groups. You must immediately report this to the Superintendent of Police along with video evidence of the speech, as it is a serious non-bailable offense under Section 196 BNS.

question: I bought an expensive asthma inhaler for my son from a local pharmacy. It turned out to be a fake expiry-tampered product, and my son had a severe asthma attack requiring hospitalization.
answer: Selling adulterated or fake medicines is a criminal offense under the BNS, not just a consumer issue. Keep the inhaler and the bill intact as evidence. File an FIR immediately against the pharmacy owner under BNS and also complain to the State Drug Controller.

question: The local Police Station Inspector flat out refused to register my FIR against a politically connected builder who grabbed my land. He verbally abused me and threw me out.
answer: If the local station refuses your FIR, you have a direct legal remedy. Draft your complaint, attach evidence, and send it via Registered Post directly to the Superintendent of Police (SP) or Commissioner of Police (CP) of your district invoking Section 173(4) BNSS.

question: Can the police just arrest me without a warrant if my neighbor files a false complaint saying I slapped him during a parking argument?
answer: For minor offenses (non-cognizable or punishable by less than 7 years, like a simple slap), the police generally cannot arrest you without a warrant from a Magistrate. They are legally mandated to first issue you a 'Notice of Appearance' (Section 35 BNSS).

question: My cousin has been inside central jail for 95 days now, but the police still haven't filed a charge sheet or submitted any final investigation report to the judge. What can we do?
answer: Your cousin is now legally entitled to 'Default Bail' (also known as Statutory Bail). If the police fail to file the charge sheet within 90 days (or 60 days depending on the crime), the court MUST grant bail regardless of the merits of the case. Your lawyer must apply immediately.

question: The police beat me up in the lockup and forced me to sign a confession paper on blank paper. Will the judge send me to jail based solely on this paper?
answer: No. Under Indian Evidence Law, any confession made to a police officer while in custody is legally inadmissible in court. It holds no evidentiary value unless that confession led the police to physically discover new evidence (like a weapon).

question: My sister committed suicide. Her husband claims she was depressed, but we know he and his parents tortured her daily for bringing a cheap car in dowry. Who has to prove she was murdered?
answer: In cases of 'Dowry Death' within 7 years of marriage, Indian evidence law specifically reverses the burden of proof. If you can show she was harassed for dowry recently, the court automatically presumes the husband/in-laws are guilty, and *they* must prove their innocence.

question: My phone lost network suddenly. Two hours later, I got an email saying my bank account was wiped clean. I found out later someone had gone to the telecom store and got a duplicate SIM issued in my name!
answer: You are a victim of 'SIM Swap Fraud'. Immediately freeze your bank accounts, notify the bank within 3 days (to ensure zero liability on you as per RBI guidelines), and register an FIR under Section 66C of the IT Act for identity theft against the fraudsters and telecom provider negligence.

question: I took a loan of 5000 rupees from a random instant loan app. Now they have hacked my contacts and are sending morphed pornographic photos of my face to my family members demanding 50,000 rupees.
answer: This is the notorious 'Loan App Extortion' scam. Do NOT pay them any more money; they will never stop. Turn off your phone, inform your family immediately that you are being blackmailed via AI deepfakes, and file a complaint firmly at 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in.
sourcePath: Section 67 & 67A, Information Technology Act, 2000 & Section 318 BNS

question: I am 8 months pregnant. I applied for my legally mandated maternity leave, but my HR manager at this private startup told me to either resign or they will terminate me tomorrow because 'they can't afford paying me to sit at home'.
answer: This is completely illegal. An employer is strictly prohibited from firing a woman on account of pregnancy or while she is on maternity leave. You have the right to 26 weeks of paid leave. You can drag the company to the Labour Commissioner and file a civil suit for compensation and reinstatement.

question: A guy from my gym has started following my auto-rickshaw every day to my office. Even when I change routes, he is there. He hasn't spoken to me, but he just stares. I feel extremely unsafe.
answer: This behavior absolutely qualifies as the criminal offense of 'Stalking' under Section 78 BNS. You do not need to wait for him to touch or speak to you. Take photos/videos of him following you, note his bike number, and file a police complaint or call the women's helpline 1091.

question: I had a confirmed flight ticket to Mumbai. At the airport, the airline staff said the flight is 'overbooked' and refused to let me board, causing me to miss a critical job interview. They offered no compensation.
answer: Airlines frequently overbook, but under DGCA guidelines, denying boarding to a confirmed passenger requires them to provide huge mandatory compensation (up to ₹20,000) immediately. Since you also missed an interview, you can file a case in the Consumer Court for 'deficiency in service' and claim heavy damages.
sourcePath: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 & DGCA CAR Guidelines

question: I bought an expensive electric scooter (EV) two months ago. Yesterday, while charging, the battery exploded and burned down half of my garage. The company says 'battery issues are not covered in warranty'.
answer: Warranty clauses do not save them from 'Product Liability'. Under the new Consumer Protection Act, if a defective product causes destruction to property or injury, the manufacturer is strictly liable to pay massive compensation. Send a legal notice demanding damages for the scooter and the garage.

question: I paid ₹1.5 Lakhs to an IAS coaching center in Karol Bagh. After three days, I realized the teachers were terrible and the AC didn't work. I asked to withdraw, but they pointed to a paper I signed saying 'Fees Once Paid is 100% Non-Refundable'.
answer: Indian Consumer Courts have repeatedly ruled that 'Fee Non-Refundable' clauses by coaching institutes are illegal and qualify as 'Unfair Trade Practices'. They can only deduct fees for the days you attended. File a case in the District Consumer Forum directly; you will win.

question: I am a landlord. My tenant has a rent agreement for 3 years, but we just signed it on a ₹100 stamp paper and had it notarized, we didn't register it in court. Now he is refusing to vacate or pay rent. Can I use the agreement to evict him?
answer: By Indian law, any lease agreement exceeding 11 months MUST be legally registered at the Sub-Registrar's office. Because yours is only notarized, it is legally invalid as a 3-year lease. Legally, it's considered a strict month-to-month tenancy, making eviction slightly different. Hire an eviction lawyer.

question: My house is at the back of a large plot. The only path to the main road goes through my neighbor's land. We have used this path for 30 years. Yesterday, he suddenly built a brick wall blocking my only exit!
answer: You have a legal 'Easement of Necessity' and possibly a 'Prescriptive Easement' (due to 30 continuous years of use). He cannot legally landlock you. Immediately file an urgent suit for 'Mandatory Injunction' in civil court to get a judge to order the wall's immediate demolition.

question: I started a small cloud kitchen from my legally owned apartment. The RWA (Resident Welfare Association) chairman is threatening to cut my water supply saying 'commercial activities are strictly banned in societies'.
answer: An RWA has no statutory power to disconnect basic amenities like water or electricity—that is illegal and a violation of your rights. However, running a cloud kitchen depends on municipal zoning laws, not just RWA rules. Send the RWA a legal notice warning against disconnecting amenities.

question: The police arrested my husband at 9 AM yesterday over a financial dispute. It has been 36 hours and they are still holding him in the police station lockup without taking him to a judge.
answer: This is entirely illegal. It is a fundamental constitutional right that an arrested person must be presented before a Magistrate within 24 hours. The police are guilty of illegal detention. Your lawyer must file an urgent Habeas Corpus petition or complain to the Magistrate immediately.

question: My husband and mother-in-law don't beat me, but they constantly taunt my skin color, tell me my parents gave them 'garbage' in dowry, and starve me for entire days if the house isn't perfectly clean. This is destroying my mental health.
answer: Cruelty is not just physical violence. Willful conduct that drives a woman to severe mental injury, deliberate starvation, and constant dowry taunts firmly fall under 'Cruelty by Husband or Relatives' (previously IPC 498A, now BNS 85/86). You can file a strong police case against them.

question: I am a YouTuber. Last night, someone bypassed my two-factor authentication, took over my entire YouTube channel, changed the password, and is livestreaming crypto scams to my 1 million subscribers!
answer: Your account has been hijacked. Do not engage with the hacker. Immediately tweet to @TeamYouTube with an alternate account, freeze linked bank/AdSense accounts, and file an FIR with the Cyber Cell under IT Act 66 for 'Computer Related Offences / Hacking'.

question: The builder promised me a flat with a 500 sq ft carpet area in the brochure and agreement. Now during handover, I measured it and it's barely 400 sq ft. He says 'super built-up area' covers the rest.
answer: Under RERA, properties can ONLY be sold based on the 'Net Carpet Area'. Selling based on ambiguous 'super built-up area' to hide a smaller flat is an illegal, deceptive practice. File a complaint with your State RERA Authority; the builder must refund the proportional money for the missing 100 sq ft.

question: An agent promised to get me a work visa for Dubai. I transferred him 3 Lakhs, he gave me a printed visa paper at the airport. At immigration, the officers told me the visa was printed on a home printer and is completely fake. The agent's phone is switched off.
answer: This is a classic 'Visa Fraud/Cheating' scheme (previously IPC 420, now under BNS 316). He has committed cheating and forgery. Keep the bank transfer receipts, WhatsApp chats, and the fake visa copy safe. Immediately lodge an FIR for criminal breach of trust and cheating with the police.

question: My neighbor has started aggressive digging right next to the common wall separating our houses to build a basement. My wall has developed massive cracks and might collapse onto my family while we sleep. The police say it's a civil property issue and won't intervene.
answer: If the police claim it's merely a civil dispute, they are ignoring the imminent danger to life. You can urgently approach the Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM) or Executive Magistrate under Section 152 of the BNSS regarding a 'public nuisance / dangerous structure'. The SDM can immediately issue orders to halt the digging.

question: My friend borrowed 5 Lakhs from me in cash two years ago. Yesterday he finally gave me a cheque, but when I deposited it, it 'bounced' because of 'Insufficient Funds'. He is now laughing at me saying I can't do anything about a friendly loan.
answer: Your friend is wrong. A bounced cheque for discharging a debt is a criminal offense under the Negotiable Instruments Act. You MUST send a formal legal notice to him within 30 days of receiving the bank memo. If he fails to pay within 15 days of the notice, file a criminal case in court.

question: My husband threw me out of his house. I am a housewife with zero income. He earns 2 Lakhs a month but claims in family court that he 'resigned' and has no job just to avoid paying me maintenance.
answer: Indian courts are strictly against this tactic. A husband's 'voluntary resignation' does not absolve him of his duty to maintain his wife. The court will look at his 'earning capacity', qualifications, and past salary, not just his current zero-income claim. File for interim maintenance under Section 125 BNSS immediately.
sourcePath: Section 125, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (formerly CrPC 125)

question: I just found out my husband has been secretly cheating on me with his colleague for 2 years. I confronted him, and now he is threatening to throw me out of the flat. The flat is registered solely in his name.
answer: He cannot throw you out. Even if the flat is 100% owned by him, because you lived there after marriage, it is legally your 'Shared Household'. You must urgently file an application under the Domestic Violence Act to get a 'Residence Order' preventing him from evicting you.
sourcePath: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005

question: I got married exactly 3 months ago. It was an arranged marriage, and I've discovered my wife is violently aggressive and lied about having severe schizophrenia. Our lives are a nightmare. The lawyer says I have to wait 1 year to file for divorce!
answer: While the general rule is a 1-year wait, there is a specific exception. Because she hid a severe mental illness and is violent, your lawyer can file an application to waive the 1-year ban citing 'Exceptional Hardship'. Gather medical proof and file immediately.

question: I worked as a lead developer at an ed-tech startup. I just quit to start my own rival ed-tech company. My old boss sent a legal notice saying my employment contract had a '2-year Non-Compete Clause' banning me from starting any competing business in India.
answer: Do not panic. In India, Post-Employment Non-Compete clauses are completely null and void under Section 27 of the Contract Act. The moment you resign, your employer cannot legally stop you from starting a rival business or joining a competitor. His legal notice is meant to scare you, it is largely unenforceable.
sourcePath: Section 28, Indian Contract Act, 1872 & Non-Compete Jurisprudence

question: My co-founder and I started a Pvt Ltd company with a 50-50 equity split. We didn't sign a founders' agreement. Now he has stopped working, refuses to talk to me, and won't resign. He still owns 50% of the company!
answer: This is a 'Founder Deadlock'. Because you didn't have a vesting schedule, you cannot automatically take back his shares, and at 50-50, you cannot vote him out of the company. You must immediately hire a corporate lawyer to attempt a buyout negotiation, or file for oppression/mismanagement in the NCLT to force a split.

question: I worked at an IT company for 5 years and 2 months. When I resigned, HR refused to pay my Gratuity, claiming 'You need 5 full years excluding notice period, and your performance was poor'.
answer: HR is legally wrong. You only need 4 years and 240 days of continuous service to be eligible for Gratuity. Performance has absolutely nothing to do with it. Send a formal legal notice; if they deny it, complain to the Controlling Authority under the Gratuity Act. They will have to pay with interest.

question: I hired a freelance designer on Fiverr to make my startup's main logo. I paid him ₹10,000. Now that my startup is famous, he is demanding ₹5 Lakhs, saying he never officially assigned the 'Copyright' of the logo to me.
answer: He is legally correct. Unlike an 'employee', a freelancer retains the copyright to their work unless you signed a specific written 'Copyright Assignment Agreement' transferring ownership to your company. Just paying him for the service is not enough. You must negotiate a buyout or redesign the logo.

question: I am a Hindu and my husband is Muslim. We married under the Special Marriage Act. Can his family force him to orally divorce me using 'Triple Talaq' to bypass the family courts?
answer: Absolutely not. Because you registered your marriage under the secular Special Marriage Act, all religious personal laws (including Triple Talaq) are completely irrelevant and legally void. Your marriage can only be dissolved by a formal decree from an Indian civil court.

question: My father gave me a lot of heavy gold jewelry during my wedding (Streedhan). Now my husband and his family have locked it all in their bank locker and refuse to give me the keys, saying it belongs to 'the family'.
answer: Gifts given to you at your wedding (Streedhan) are your absolute personal property. Your husband/in-laws are merely 'trustees' of it. Refusing to return your Streedhan when demanded is a criminal breach of trust under the BNS. File an FIR immediately and claim it back.

question: My ex-wife has primary custody of our 8-year-old son. She has suddenly moved to a different state 1000 km away and blocked my number, completely violating my court-ordered weekend visitation rights. The local police say they can't help.
answer: The police are right, this is not a criminal matter yet, it is 'Contempt of Court'. Your ex-wife has deliberately violated the family court's specific visitation order. You must urgently file a Contempt Petition in the family court that originally granted custody. The judge can fine her, order police to fetch the child, or even reverse custody to you.

question: A vendor gave my startup a post-dated cheque for ₹2 Lakhs. When I deposited it, it bounced. But my accountant made a mistake and only informed me about the bounce 45 days later. Now the vendor says I missed the legal deadline to sue him.
answer: The vendor is partly correct; you missed the strict 30-day window to send a legal notice for a criminal cheque bounce case (Section 138). However, the debt is NOT dead. You can still file a civil suit for recovery of money, or re-present the cheque to the bank (if it's still within its 3-month validity period) and start the 30-day clock fresh when it bounces again.

question: My D2C coffee brand is called 'BrewZing'. We have a registered trademark. A huge FMCG company just launched an energy drink called 'BrewZinger' with an almost identical font and logo colors. My business will be destroyed.
answer: This is a textbook case of 'Trademark Infringement' and 'Passing Off' (creating deceptive similarity). Because your mark is registered, you have immediate legal power. Hire an IP lawyer urgently to file a suit in the High Court for an 'ex-parte injunction'. The court can order them to immediately halt all sales and recall their products.

question: My husband filed for divorce. I am fighting the case, but I have no income to even pay my lawyer's fees or travel to the court. My husband says it's my problem.
answer: Your husband is wrong. Under Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act, if you do not have an independent income, the court will force your husband to pay for ALL your litigation expenses (lawyer fees, travel costs) AND a monthly allowance while the case is ongoing. File a Section 24 application immediately.

question: I work in an IT company. Yesterday, the CEO suddenly called 50 of us into a room, took our laptops, and told us we are fired effective immediately because the company has 'no funds'. No notice period, no severance.
answer: This is an illegal mass layoff ('Retrenchment'). If you have worked there for over 1 year, the company is legally mandated to give you 1 month's notice (or pay in lieu) AND retrenchment compensation (15 days pay for every year worked). You group together and file a complaint with the joint Labour Commissioner immediately.
sourcePath: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 & State Shops and Establishments Act

question: I am a 70-year-old widow. I legally gifted my house to my son on the condition he would take care of me. Now he and his wife have stopped giving me food and are forcing me to live in the damp basement.
answer: You have a powerful remedy. Under the Senior Citizens Act, if a child fails to provide basic care after taking property via gift/transfer, the 'Maintenance Tribunal' (chaired by the SDM) can legally cancel the gift deed, declare it void due to fraud, and forcefully evict your son. Go directly to the local SDM office.
sourcePath: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007

question: My cousin got involved with a group that extorts money and runs illegal businesses. He was just a driver, not directly involved in the violence, but now the police are saying he's part of an 'organized crime syndicate.' What does this mean under the new laws, and what are his chances if he wasn't directly committing the main offenses?
answer: Under the new BNS, involvement in an 'organized crime syndicate' is a very serious charge. Even if your cousin wasn't directly committing acts of violence or main offenses, simply being a member, assisting, or facilitating the syndicate's activities (like driving for them knowing their purpose) can lead to severe penalties. The law targets the entire network. If someone is part of such a syndicate and causes death, they can face life imprisonment or even the death penalty. For other involvements, the punishment can range from five years to life imprisonment, along with fines. It's crucial for your cousin to get strong legal representation to prove the extent of his involvement and intent, or lack thereof.

question: Someone opened multiple fake bank accounts and credit cards using my Aadhaar and PAN details, which I accidentally shared on a phishing link. Now I'm getting notices for loans I never took. Can the new laws help me prove I'm a victim of identity theft, and what recourse do I have against these fraudsters?
answer: Yes, the BNS provides strong provisions to address such frauds. Your situation would primarily be considered 'cheating by personation,' where someone pretends to be you to gain a benefit, like opening accounts or taking loans. This carries a punishment of up to three years imprisonment or a fine, or both. Additionally, depending on how your data was misused, other sections related to fraud and the Information Technology Act, 2000, could also apply, potentially increasing the severity of the charges against the fraudsters. You should immediately file a police complaint, ideally with the cybercrime unit, and inform all affected banks and credit agencies to dispute the fraudulent transactions.

question: My neighbor's son got into a fight with a few local boys and caused minor injuries. The police are saying it's not a very serious offense, but they might involve the new law's 'community service' punishment. What exactly is community service as a punishment under BNS, and for what types of offenses can it be given?
answer: Community service is a new type of punishment introduced by the BNS for less serious, or 'petty,' offenses. Instead of sending someone to jail or imposing a fine, the court can order the offender to perform unpaid work for the benefit of the community for a specified period. This could involve tasks like cleaning public places, assisting in community centers, or environmental work. For offenses causing minor injuries, if it's considered a petty offense, community service could be an option. It's meant to reform offenders and make them contribute positively to society, rather than just punishing them with incarceration or fines.

question: My brother was attacked by a mob of people from another community in our village over a rumor. He's badly injured. The police initially registered it as just 'assault.' With the new laws, isn't there something specific about mob violence or hate crimes? What should we push the police to investigate under the BNS?
answer: Yes, the new BNS has specific provisions concerning mob violence, particularly when it's driven by discriminatory motives, often referred to as 'hate crimes.' While Section 103(2) directly addresses mob lynching leading to death, the spirit of this law aims to treat mob attacks based on community, caste, or other similar grounds with extreme seriousness. Even if it's not a case of murder, the fact that a 'group of five or more persons acting in concert' attacked your brother over a rumor targeting his community, leading to 'bad injuries,' means the police should investigate it as an aggravated offense of grievous hurt (which also has severe penalties under BNS) committed by a mob, with the intent to highlight the discriminatory nature. You should insist that the police consider the 'mob' and 'community-based' aspects during their investigation, as these factors lead to much harsher punishments for the perpetrators under BNS.

question: My friend tried to break into a shop but was caught before he could actually steal anything. He's being charged with 'attempt to commit an offence.' Is this the same as if he had actually stolen something? What's the punishment for just an 'attempt' under the new BNS?
answer: No, an 'attempt' is generally not punished as severely as a completed offense, but it is still a serious crime under the BNS. For most offenses, if someone attempts to commit it but fails, and there isn't a specific punishment defined for that particular 'attempt' (like for murder or dacoity), then the person can be punished with up to half of the maximum imprisonment prescribed for the completed offense, or with a fine, or both. So, for an attempt to commit theft (which has a maximum of three years imprisonment), your friend could face up to one and a half years in prison, or a fine, or both, even though he didn't actually steal anything. The 'act towards the commission' is what makes the attempt punishable.

question: My cousin got involved with a local gang that extorts money from small businesses in our area. He claims he just helps with logistics and never directly threatens anyone. If the police catch them, will he also face serious charges, even if he wasn't involved in the violence?
answer: Yes, your cousin can face very serious charges. Under the new BNS, being a member of an organised crime syndicate, even if not directly involved in every violent act, is a major offense. Simply assisting with the syndicate's activities, like logistics for extortion, can lead to severe punishment, including minimum five years to life imprisonment and hefty fines.

question: In our village, there was a rumour that a man stole a motorcycle. A group of about ten people surrounded him and beat him severely. Some people, including me, just watched from a distance without participating. What are the legal consequences for everyone involved, especially for those who only observed but didn't physically assault him?
answer: This act would be classified as 'mob lynching' under BNS, which is a very serious crime. Anyone who is part of the group of five or more persons acting together to commit such violence, even if they didn't personally inflict injuries, can be held liable. The punishment can be as severe as life imprisonment or even death for those directly involved, and significant prison terms for others in the group.

question: My younger brother was going through a tough time and attempted to take his own life. The police were called. Will he be arrested or charged with a crime for attempting suicide now? Also, his online 'friend' was constantly encouraging him to do it; can that person be punished?
answer: No, your brother will not be arrested or charged for attempting suicide. The BNS has decriminalized this act. Instead, the focus will be on providing him support. However, the person who encouraged or incited him to attempt suicide can face severe criminal charges under 'abetment of suicide'. If your brother's attempt was a consequence of that encouragement, the 'friend' could face up to ten years in prison and a fine.

question: My ex-boyfriend is harassing me online by sending unsolicited explicit images, posting my private photos (taken without my consent) on a shared cloud drive, and constantly sending threatening messages. Is this a crime under the new laws, and what can I do?
answer: Yes, this is definitely a crime under the new BNS. Your ex-boyfriend's actions fall directly under 'Sexual harassment by electronic means'. Sending explicit images, sharing your private photos without consent, and sending threatening messages online are all punishable offenses. You should immediately report this to the police, providing all available evidence like screenshots and message logs. He could face up to three years in prison and a fine.

question: A competitor has been spreading false rumors publicly that my business uses substandard materials and cheats customers, causing significant loss of reputation and clients. Can I file a criminal case for defamation against them under the new BNS, and what kind of proof would I need?
answer: Yes, you can file a criminal case for defamation under BNS Section 356. Spreading false rumors that harm your business's reputation and cause financial losses clearly falls under this definition. You would need proof of the false statements being made (e.g., recordings, witness testimonies, published articles, social media posts) and evidence that these statements have damaged your reputation and business. The competitor could face up to two years in prison, a fine, or both.

question: My son was pressured by some local goons to store a package for them, which he didn't know contained illegal goods. He only did it once out of fear. Now the police are saying he's part of an 'organised crime syndicate' and he could face very serious charges. Is just storing something once enough to be charged with organised crime under the new law? What does this mean for him?
answer: Under the new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 'organised crime' is a very serious offense. Even if your son was only involved once, if the police can prove he was part of a group of two or more people who committed illegal acts for profit, and he knowingly participated in some way, even under pressure, he could be charged. The law covers a wide range of activities. The minimum punishment for organised crime is five years in jail, which can go up to life imprisonment, along with a fine. It's crucial to seek immediate legal counsel to understand the specific evidence against him and build a strong defense.

question: My brother was involved in an argument that escalated into a street fight. A crowd gathered, and in the chaos, some people beat up the other party, who unfortunately died. My brother admits he was there and maybe pushed someone, but he insists he never intended to kill anyone and wasn't part of the main group that caused the fatal injuries. The police are saying this is a 'mob lynching' case and he faces life imprisonment or even death. What does the new law say about this?
answer: The new BNS has a specific, very serious provision for murder committed by a group of five or more people acting together, especially if it's based on certain discriminatory grounds. If your brother was part of a group of five or more, and that group committed murder, even if he didn't directly cause the death or intend it, he could be held equally responsible with others in that group if they were 'acting in concert'. The punishment for this specific offense is either life imprisonment or the death penalty, along with a fine. It is critical to establish his exact role, whether he was acting 'in concert' with the main group, and if the specific discriminatory grounds alleged by the police apply. You need an immediate lawyer.

question: My girlfriend and I were in a relationship for two years. He repeatedly promised to marry me, even introducing me to his family. Based on these promises, I had sexual relations with him. Now he's suddenly broken up with me and refuses to marry, saying he never seriously intended to. Can I file a police complaint under the new law, or is this just a civil matter of a broken promise?
answer: Yes, under the new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), it is now a specific criminal offense if a man has sexual intercourse with a woman by making a promise to marry her, but without any real intention of fulfilling that promise. This is not just a civil matter anymore. If you can prove that he made a false promise to marry with no intention of following through, and you had sexual intercourse with him because of that false promise, he could face imprisonment for up to ten years and a fine. You can certainly file a police complaint, and it's advisable to gather any evidence you have of his promises (messages, photos, witnesses).

question: My teenage son got caught trying to steal a cheap mobile phone from a local shop. He's never been in trouble before, and it was a silly mistake he deeply regrets. The shopkeeper is willing to drop charges if my son apologizes and works at his shop for a few days. Under the new laws, can he avoid jail time or a heavy fine, maybe by doing some community service instead, since it's his first offense and for a small amount?
answer: Yes, under the new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), for certain less serious offenses, especially if it's a first-time offense and the punishment is less than three years in jail, the court now has the option to order 'community service' instead of imprisonment or a heavy fine. This means your son might be asked to do unpaid work for the public good, like helping at an old age home or cleaning public spaces. This is a progressive change aimed at reforming offenders rather than just punishing them. The specific section for theft (BNS Section 303) combined with the general provisions for community service makes it possible. It is a good sign that the shopkeeper is also open to an alternative resolution. You should definitely discuss this possibility with your lawyer and the prosecution.

question: Someone created a fake social media profile using my name and photos, and is posting offensive content pretending to be me. They even gained access to an old email account of mine and sent malicious emails to my professional contacts. This is damaging my reputation. Is this just cyberbullying, or is there a specific criminal charge under the new BNS for this kind of digital identity theft?
answer: This is much more than just cyberbullying; it's a serious criminal offense called 'identity theft' under the new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). The law specifically covers someone fraudulently using your name, photos, electronic signature, or any unique identity information to impersonate you, make false representations, or commit other offenses. This includes creating fake social media profiles or accessing your email to send malicious content. The person responsible could face imprisonment for up to three years, a fine of up to one lakh rupees, or both. You should immediately report this to the police, providing all evidence of the fake profiles, malicious emails, and any other misuse of your identity.

question: My younger brother got involved with a group that was running an illegal online gambling operation. He claims he only handled the technical backend, like managing servers and payment gateways, and wasn't directly involved in threatening people or collecting money. Can he still be charged under 'Organised Crime' under the new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, even if he didn't commit any violence himself?
answer: Yes, under the new BNS, your brother can indeed be charged under 'Organised Crime' even if he didn't directly commit violent acts. The law is very broad and covers anyone who is part of an 'organised crime syndicate' and facilitates or aids any continuous unlawful activity carried out by them, even if his role is only technical or supportive. The focus is on being part of the syndicate and contributing to its unlawful objectives, which in this case involves gaining economic advantage through illegal gambling. The penalties for organised crime are very severe.

question: Someone created a fake profile on Instagram using my exact name, photos, and personal details. They are now messaging my friends, pretending to be me, and asking for money claiming it's an emergency. What specific crime have they committed under the new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, and how serious is it?
answer: The person who created the fake profile and is asking for money pretending to be you has committed the specific offense of 'Cheating by Personation' under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. This is a serious offense, as it involves impersonating someone else to deceive for financial gain. The person can face imprisonment for up to three years, a fine, or both, upon conviction.

question: My friend recently attempted to take their own life but was fortunately saved by family members. The police arrived, but instead of arresting them, they suggested professional counselling. I remember attempting suicide used to be a crime. Is it still punishable under the new BNS, or have the laws changed significantly? And what if I had encouraged them?
answer: Under the new legal framework in India, attempting to take one's own life is no longer considered a crime. Instead, the law presumes the person is under severe stress and prioritizes mental health support and care. So, your friend will not be prosecuted or arrested for the attempt itself, and the police's suggestion for counselling is correct. However, if you or anyone else had encouraged or helped your friend to attempt suicide, that would be a very serious criminal offense called 'Abetment of Suicide' under BNS, carrying a potential punishment of up to ten years in prison and a fine.

question: My cousin was tragically killed by a group of six people in a village, apparently because of a misunderstanding about his religious symbols. I heard about new provisions in BNS regarding 'mob lynching'. How does this specific provision affect the charges and potential punishment for the attackers compared to a regular murder charge?
answer: Under the new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), the murder of your cousin falls under a very specific and serious provision designed to tackle 'mob lynching' or hate crimes. Because a group of six people committed the murder on the grounds of his personal belief (religious symbols), each and every member of that group can face extremely severe punishment – either the death penalty or imprisonment for life, in addition to a fine. This provision is distinct from general murder charges, as it specifically targets group violence motivated by prejudice, ensuring harsher penalties for all involved.

question: I was walking down the street when someone on a scooter suddenly rode past and snatched my mobile phone right out of my hand. They didn't push me or physically harm me, just grabbed the phone and sped off. Is this still just considered 'theft' under the new BNS, or is there a specific, more serious crime for this act of 'snatching'?
answer: Under the new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), the act you described is no longer just classified as 'theft'. It is now recognized as a distinct and more serious offense called 'Snatching' under Section 304. Even though no physical harm or wrongful restraint was caused, the act of suddenly or forcibly taking property from a person makes it 'snatching'. This specific crime carries a punishment of imprisonment up to three years, along with a fine, making it a more severe offense than basic theft.

question: My friend was arrested for a serious assault case, which could lead to over 7 years in jail. The police haven't done any forensic examination of the crime scene yet, saying they don't have enough resources. Under the new laws, isn't it mandatory for them to involve forensic experts for such serious crimes?
answer: Yes, under the new criminal procedure law (BNSS), for any crime where the punishment can be 7 years imprisonment or more, it is now mandatory for forensic experts to visit the crime scene and collect evidence. This process must also be videographed. Even if your state lacks such facilities, they must use those available in another state. So, the police cannot skip this step for a serious assault case simply due to resource issues.

question: My brother was called to the police station for questioning as a suspect in a cheating case. He's worried the police might misrepresent his statement. He heard about new rules regarding recording statements. Is there anything in the BNSS that ensures his statement is recorded properly, maybe through video?
answer: Under the new BNSS law, whenever an accused person's statement is recorded by the police, it should ideally be done using audio-visual electronic means (like video recording). While it's not strictly mandatory in every single instance, the law requires the police to provide a written reason if they don't use audio-visual recording. This provision aims to increase transparency and reduce the chances of misrepresentation, so your brother can request for his statement to be recorded this way.

question: My neighbor, who was accused of a serious fraud, absconded almost a year ago and hasn't been seen since. I heard that under the new criminal laws, cases can now proceed even if the accused is not present. Can his trial actually start and conclude without him ever appearing in court?
answer: Yes, under the new BNSS, a trial can indeed proceed without your neighbor being present if he is declared an 'absconder' and has evaded arrest for at least 180 days after charges were framed or a charge-sheet filed. The court must be convinced that he is intentionally avoiding justice. If the trial concludes in his absence, the judgment, whether conviction or acquittal, will be fully valid and enforceable, meaning he could be convicted and sentenced even without ever appearing in court.

question: I received a court summons for a minor complaint via WhatsApp and also an email. My friend says it's not official unless it's a physical paper. Is service through digital platforms like WhatsApp or email now considered legally valid under the new Indian criminal procedure law?
answer: Yes, under the new BNSS, the court can legally send you official summons and even arrest warrants through electronic means like email, WhatsApp, or other instant messaging services. This is a significant change. As long as there's a verifiable record of the message being sent and delivered, and the court is satisfied that you're likely to receive it through that digital contact, it's considered valid service. So, the digital summons you received is likely legitimate and should not be ignored.
sourcePath: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) Sections 64 and 69

question: My sister filed an FIR for a serious robbery six months ago, but we haven't heard anything from the police since then. We feel completely in the dark about the investigation. Do we, as the victims, have any right to regularly know the status of the investigation under the new criminal procedure laws?
answer: Yes, absolutely! Under the new BNSS, victims have a clear right to be informed about the progress of the investigation. The police are now legally required to inform you, the victim, about the status of the investigation within 90 days of filing the FIR. If the investigation isn't completed within that initial 90-day period, the police must continue to provide updates every 90 days until the case is closed. You can contact the police station and demand this information, citing Section 193(3) of BNSS.

question: I'm a victim of persistent cyberstalking and online harassment, which doesn't involve physical threat but has severely impacted my mental peace. The police station asked me to file a 'preliminary complaint' online first and said they would assess if an FIR is needed, instead of registering it immediately. Is this new process correct under the law, especially when I want to report it instantly using their online portal?
answer: Yes, under the new BNSS, for certain offenses (those punishable with 3 to less than 7 years of imprisonment, like some forms of cyberstalking), the police are now legally required to conduct a 'preliminary enquiry' within 14 days before registering a formal FIR. This is to quickly determine if there's enough initial evidence to warrant a full investigation. You can definitely file your complaint electronically through their online portal as allowed by law, and the police will then initiate this preliminary enquiry based on your submission.
sourcePath: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) Sections 173 and 175

question: My relative was found dead in suspicious circumstances, possibly due to poisoning, which is a serious crime. The local police have taken the body for post-mortem but haven't mentioned involving any advanced forensic team or collecting specialized evidence from the scene. Don't the new laws make forensic investigation mandatory for such grave offenses?
answer: Yes, you are correct. Under the new BNSS, if the suspected crime (like poisoning leading to death) carries a punishment of seven years or more imprisonment, it is now legally mandatory for a forensic expert to visit the crime scene and collect forensic evidence. You should insist that the police comply with this provision and ensure a forensic team is involved for a thorough investigation, as this evidence is crucial.

question: My brother has been in judicial custody for 110 days for a non-heinous economic offense. The police still haven't filed a chargesheet. Also, we were told that the police are supposed to provide all case documents electronically, but we haven't received anything. What are his rights regarding bail and access to documents under the new law?
answer: Your brother has significant rights under the new law. Firstly, since the chargesheet hasn't been filed within 90 days for an offense not punishable with death, life imprisonment, or 10 years or more, he is now legally entitled to 'default bail'. This means he must be released on bail, regardless of the merits of the case, if he applies for it. Secondly, the police were indeed supposed to provide him with all case documents, including the chargesheet, in electronic format, within 60 days from his first appearance in court. You should immediately move for default bail and demand the electronic supply of documents.
sourcePath: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) Sections 230 and 236

question: My neighbor was declared a 'proclaimed offender' a few years ago under the old law for a property fraud case. He briefly returned, but after a new complaint was lodged against him for another fraud, he has absconded again. Can the court now proceed with his trial for the old case, or even the new one, even if he's not present and can't be found?
answer: Yes, under the new BNSS, the court can now proceed with your neighbor's trial even in his absence, a concept called 'trial in absentia'. Since he was already declared a proclaimed offender and has now absconded again to avoid legal proceedings, the court can, after explaining its reasons, record evidence and conduct the trial as if he were present, eventually leading to a judgment. This applies to both the old and new cases if the conditions are met.
sourcePath: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) Sections 82 and 356

question: I received an official-looking WhatsApp message from the police requesting my presence as a witness for a case. They also mentioned that if I can't come in person, they might record my statement via a video call. Is this a legitimate way for the police to summon me or record my statement, or is it a scam?
answer: This is legitimate under the new BNSS. The law now permits police to send summonses through electronic means, including instant messaging services like WhatsApp, as long as it's an official communication. Furthermore, they are also legally allowed to record your statement as a witness during an investigation using audio-video electronic means (like a video call). So, while you should always verify the sender's identity to avoid scams, the methods mentioned are permissible under current Indian law.
sourcePath: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) Sections 199 and 202

question: An ex-employee from my IT startup downloaded critical client databases and proprietary source code before leaving. Now, I suspect they are using this data to start a competing venture. What legal steps can I take under Indian cyber law to stop them and recover damages?
answer: If an ex-employee has unlawfully accessed, copied, or used your company's digital data, it constitutes a cybercrime under the IT Act. You can file a complaint with the cyber cell. You may claim damages for the financial loss suffered due to their actions under Section 43 and they can face criminal penalties including imprisonment and fines under Section 66. It's crucial to gather all evidence related to the data theft, such as logs or forensic reports.

question: Someone created a fake Instagram profile using my exact name, photos, and even my professional designation. They are using it to post derogatory comments about my workplace and family. How can I get this profile removed and press charges against the person responsible?
answer: Creating a fake online profile to impersonate you, especially to defame you, is a serious cybercrime. Section 66C of the IT Act specifically addresses identity theft, while Section 66D covers cheating by personation using a computer. You should immediately report the fake profile to Instagram's support and also file a complaint with the local cybercrime cell. The perpetrator, if identified, can face significant imprisonment and fines.

question: Our small manufacturing business has been hit by a ransomware attack. All our production data and accounting files are encrypted, and we see a message demanding payment in cryptocurrency to unlock them. Is this a criminal offense in India, and what are the legal steps we should take?
answer: A ransomware attack is unequivocally a criminal offense under the IT Act. The act of introducing malicious software (ransomware) and disrupting your computer systems constitutes damage under Section 43, for which the perpetrator can be punished under Section 66. You should immediately report the incident to the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) and your local cybercrime police. Do not pay the ransom without expert advice, as there's no guarantee your data will be restored, and it may further fund criminal activities.

question: After a bad breakup, my ex-boyfriend posted a private, intimate video of me on a public adult website without my consent. I'm terrified and humiliated. What specific legal action can I take in India to have it removed and prosecute him?
answer: What your ex-boyfriend has done is a severe cybercrime known as 'revenge porn' under Section 67A of the IT Act. This section specifically criminalizes the non-consensual publication or transmission of sexually explicit material. You should immediately contact the cybercrime police and file a First Information Report (FIR). They can initiate action to have the content removed and prosecute your ex, who faces significant imprisonment and fines. Preserve any evidence you have, like screenshots or links, but do not share the explicit content further.

question: I received SMS alerts about several unauthorized transactions from my bank account, totaling Rs. 50,000. I did not share my OTP or any details with anyone, but I remember clicking a suspicious link yesterday. What are the legal steps I need to take to recover my money and complain about this cyber fraud?
answer: This is a clear case of online banking fraud, a serious cybercrime. Your immediate actions are crucial: 1. Block your bank account/card. 2. Inform your bank immediately (within 3 days for potential zero liability). 3. File a complaint with the cybercrime police (online at www.cybercrime.gov.in or at your local cyber cell). The perpetrator, if caught, can face charges under the IT Act for unauthorized access, computer-related offenses, and potentially identity theft. Act quickly to maximize your chances of recovering funds.
sourcePath: Information Technology Act, 2000, Section 43, 66, 66C; RBI Guidelines on Customer Liability in Unauthorized Electronic Banking Transactions

question: Consumer rights overview
answer:
Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, Indian law guarantees 6 core consumer rights:
• Right to Safety & Information: Protection against hazardous goods and complete transparency regarding price, purity, and expiry dates.
• Right to Choose & Be Heard: Freedom to select competitive products and represent your grievances before forums.
• Right to Redressal & Education: Legal entitlement to refund, replacement, or compensation for defective items or deficient services via the National Consumer Helpline (1915) or e-Daakhil portal.

question: An e-commerce website refuses to refund my money for a damaged phone delivered in an open box, citing their no-return policy.
answer:
A 'no-return policy' cannot override statutory law. Under the E-Commerce Rules 2020:
• You are legally entitled to a 100% refund or replacement for damaged, defective, or misdescribed products.
• The seller/platform cannot impose arbitrary cancellation or refusal charges.
• You can immediately lodge a complaint on the National Consumer Helpline (Call 1915 or WhatsApp 8800001915) or file on e-Daakhil.

question: What are the pecuniary limits and where can I file a consumer court case in India?
answer:
The Consumer Protection Act establishes a three-tier dispute redressal system based on claim value:
• District Commission: Handles claims up to ₹50 Lakhs.
• State Commission: Handles claims from ₹50 Lakhs up to ₹2 Crores.
• National Commission (NCDRC): Handles claims exceeding ₹2 Crores.
• You can file complaints online from anywhere in India using the e-Daakhil portal (edaakhil.nic.in) without hiring a lawyer.

question: A pressure cooker exploded in my kitchen causing severe burn injuries due to a manufacturing flaw. Can I sue the manufacturer for damages?
answer:
Yes, under the 'Product Liability' provisions of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019:
• The manufacturer and seller are strictly liable to pay compensation for physical injuries, medical expenses, and property damage caused by a defective product.
• You do not need to prove negligence—proof of defect and resulting harm is sufficient.
• Preserve the damaged appliance, hospital medical bills, and purchase receipt to claim compensation before the District Consumer Commission.

question: An airline cancelled my flight at the last minute without offering alternative booking or hotel stay. Can I claim compensation for deficiency of service?
answer:
Yes, last-minute flight cancellations without support constitute 'Deficiency of Service':
• Under DGCA Passenger Charter and CPA 2019, the airline must offer an alternate flight or full immediate refund plus compensation up to ₹10,000 depending on flight duration.
• You can claim reimbursement for hotel stay, food, and wasted connecting bookings.
• File an immediate grievance on AirSewa portal (airsewa.gov.in) and National Consumer Helpline (1915).

question: A coaching institute charged ₹1.5 lakh full two-year fees upfront and refused to refund any money when I quit after one month due to substandard teaching.
answer:
The coaching institute cannot forfeit the entire fee:
• Consumer courts and CCPA guidelines strictly hold that charging fees for future unavailed months/years is an illegal unfair trade practice.
• The institute must refund the proportionate fee for the remaining duration after deducting a reasonable registration charge.
• Send a formal legal notice for refund; if unfulfilled, file a complaint on e-Daakhil for refund plus mental agony damages.
sourcePath: Section 2(47), Consumer Protection Act, 2019 & CCPA Guidelines 2022

question: A beauty product advertised '100% hair regrowth in 14 days' with celebrity endorsement, but it caused allergic scalp burn. Can I sue for misleading advertisement?
answer:
Yes, this falls under 'Misleading Advertisements and False Guarantees':
• The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) can fine both the manufacturer and the celebrity endorser up to ₹10 Lakhs.
• You can file a complaint with the National Consumer Helpline and before the Consumer Commission for medical compensation and refund.
• Keep photographs of the scalp injury, the advertisement screenshot, and dermatologist prescription.

question: A health insurance company rejected my cashless hospital claim citing a generic non-existent pre-existing disease clause.
answer:
Arbitrary repudiation of genuine medical claims is a recognized 'Deficiency of Service':
• Under IRDAI regulations, an insurer cannot reject a claim unless they have tangible clinical proof of pre-existing condition non-disclosure.
• After 8 years of continuous coverage (moratorium period), policies cannot be questioned for pre-existing disease.
• Escalate to the Insurance Ombudsman (cioins.co.in) within 1 year or file before the District Consumer Commission.
sourcePath: Section 2(11), Consumer Protection Act, 2019 & IRDAI Regulations

question: What are dark patterns in online shopping apps, and are they illegal under Indian consumer law?
answer:
Dark patterns are manipulative design tricks used by apps to cheat consumers, and they are strictly illegal in India:
• Common illegal tricks: False urgency ('Only 2 left in stock!'), basket sneaking (automatically adding insurance or donation fees to cart), and hidden cancellation buttons.
• CCPA guidelines categorize these as Unfair Trade Practices under Section 2(47).
• You can report deceptive apps directly to the National Consumer Helpline (1915) or CCPA.

question: A builder delayed flat possession by 4 years despite taking 95% payment. Can I approach the Consumer Court instead of RERA?
answer:
Yes, homebuyers can approach either Consumer Court or RERA:
• The Supreme Court affirmed that CPA 2019 and RERA are concurrent remedies—you are free to choose the Consumer Commission.
• You can claim full refund of money paid along with 9%–12% annual interest or monthly delayed compensation.
• If the property value plus compensation is under ₹50 Lakhs, file in District Commission; between ₹50 Lakhs and ₹2 Crores in State Commission.

question: I found a dead insect in a meal delivered by a restaurant through Zomato/Swiggy. What can I do legally?
answer:
• Legal Rights: Under Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 & Section 2(47) CPA 2019, consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.
• Recommended Action: Report immediately to FSSAI (Consumer Grievance Portal) and file for compensation on e-Daakhil for health hazard and deficiency of service. Preserve the food sample and photo.
• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).
sourcePath: Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 & Section 2(47) CPA 2019

question: A brand new car has recurring engine failure within 3 months, and the service center refuses to replace the vehicle.
answer:
• Legal Rights: Under Section 84, Consumer Protection Act, 2019, consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.
• Recommended Action: Recurring manufacturing defects within warranty qualify for vehicle replacement or full refund under Product Liability (Section 84 CPA 2019). File before State or District Commission.
• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).

question: A courier service lost my laptop parcel containing important documents and offered only ₹100 standard compensation.
answer:
• Legal Rights: Under Carriers Act & Section 2(11) CPA 2019, consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.
• Recommended Action: Standard low-liability clauses on courier receipts cannot evade liability for gross negligence. Consumer courts award market value of goods plus compensation for deficiency of service.
• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).

question: A dry cleaner bleached and ruined my silk designer wedding saree worth ₹60,000.
answer:
• Legal Rights: Under Section 2(11), Consumer Protection Act, 2019, consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.
• Recommended Action: Service providers are bailment custodians and must compensate for the full market depreciation/value of ruined garments. Do not accept token ₹100 coupons; send legal notice.
• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).

question: A private hospital charged ₹30,000 above the government mandated ceiling rate for oxygen and medicines.
answer:
• Legal Rights: Under Clinical Establishments Act & CPA 2019, consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.
• Recommended Action: Overcharging beyond government price caps or MRP constitutes an unfair trade practice. File complaint with District Consumer Forum and state health authority for full refund with penalty.
• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).

question: My debit card was charged ₹45,000 internationally without any OTP or alert. Will the bank reimburse me?
answer:
• Legal Rights: Under RBI Circular on Limiting Customer Liability (2017), consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.
• Recommended Action: If reported within 3 days of unauthorized transaction, customer liability is ZERO under RBI rules. If the bank fails to reverse within 10 days, escalate to the Banking Ombudsman.
• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).
sourcePath: RBI Circular on Limiting Customer Liability (2017)

question: Despite DND activation, I receive 20 telemarketing spam calls daily and zero mobile network in my residence.
answer:
• Legal Rights: Under TRAI Regulations & CPA 2019, consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.
• Recommended Action: Violations of TRAI UCC regulations attract penalties against telemarketers. You can file complaint on TRAI DND 3.0 app and claim damages for deficient telecom service before consumer forum.
• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).

question: A supermarket sold packaged baby milk powder with an expired date label pasted over with a fresh sticker.
answer:
• Legal Rights: Under Consumer Protection Act, 2019 & Legal Metrology Act, consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.
• Recommended Action: Tampering with expiry dates is a serious criminal offence under FSSAI and an unfair trade practice under CPA 2019. The store manager can face fines and prosecution.
• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).
sourcePath: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 & Legal Metrology Act

question: Electricity board issued a false bill of ₹80,000 for a locked vacant flat and threatened disconnection.
answer:
• Legal Rights: Under Electricity Act, 2003 & Consumer Protection Act, consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.
• Recommended Action: You can challenge the arbitrary bill before the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum (CGRF) of the electricity board. Supply cannot be disconnected while a bona fide dispute is pending.
• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).

question: My train was cancelled due to fog, but IRCTC did not automatically refund my Tatkal ticket amount.
answer:
• Legal Rights: Under Indian Railways Consumer Rules & CPA 2019, consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.
• Recommended Action: For train cancellation by Railways, full fare refund is automatic. If IRCTC system fails, file a TDR (Ticket Deposit Receipt) within 72 hours. Failure to refund is actionable under CPA 2019.
• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).

question: My trolley bag was broken and contents stolen during transit on an Indigo flight.
answer:
• Legal Rights: Under Carriage by Air Act & DGCA Rules, consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.

• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).

question: A shopping mall charged ₹150 parking fee for purchasing goods worth ₹5,000 in their retail stores.
answer:
• Legal Rights: Under Consumer Protection Act & State Mall Guidelines, consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.

• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).
sourcePath: Consumer Protection Act & State Mall Guidelines

question: Television manufacturer refuses to repair screen stating spare parts are discontinued after only 18 months.
answer:

• Recommended Action: Under the Indian Right to Repair framework and CPA 2019, manufacturers must maintain spare parts and provide repair service for the reasonable lifespan of consumer appliances.
• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).

question: Bank issued an unsolicited credit card, activated it without OTP, and charged an annual fee of ₹3,000.
answer:
• Legal Rights: Under RBI Master Direction on Credit & Debit Cards (2022), consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.

• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).
sourcePath: RBI Master Direction on Credit & Debit Cards (2022)

question: I paid ₹4,000 for annual maintenance of water filter, but no technician visited despite 10 complaints.
answer:

• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).

question: A fitness center collected 1-year advance membership fees of ₹25,000 and shut down permanently within 2 weeks.

• Legal Rights: Under Section 2(47), Consumer Protection Act, 2019, consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.

question: Authorized smartphone service center charged original part price but installed a cheap duplicate battery that swelled.

question: Gold ring purchased with 22K hallmark tested at only 18K purity at a government assaying center.

• Legal Rights: Under Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) Act, 2016, consumers are protected against deficient service and defective goods.

• Dispute Redressal: Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or file complaint digitally on e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in).

question: Airline charged double the published per-kg excess baggage rate at the check-in counter.

question: Multiplex theater charged ₹120 for a ₹20 MRP mineral water bottle and prohibited bringing personal water inside.

question: A diagnostic lab falsely reported positive HIV result causing severe trauma, later disproved by 3 other labs.

question: Hotel refused cancellation refund when city was under government flood lockdown emergency.

Yes, maintenance is a statutory right under Section 144 BNSS:
• A wife who does not have independent sufficient income and minor children are entitled to monthly maintenance commensurate with husband's lifestyle and earning capacity.
• The court can grant Interim Maintenance within 60 days of notice to ensure immediate survival while the petition is contested.
• Non-payment of ordered maintenance results in warrants and imprisonment of the husband until dues are cleared.

question: My landlord cut off our electricity and water supply because I refused an arbitrary 30% mid-tenancy rent hike. Can he do this?
answer:

• Landlords cannot withhold essential civic amenities (water, electricity, lift access) under any circumstances, even during dispute or non-payment of rent.
• You can file an emergency petition before the Rent Authority / Civil Magistrate, who will restore utilities within 24 hours and penalize the landlord.
• You can also lodge a police complaint for criminal harassment and wrongful restraint.
